stops.campa: He is sent to Clifton College, a boarding school on the high ground above Bristol, in the city where his father works on beetles at the university below. A school friend tells him that memory might work the way a hologram does: spread across the whole plate rather than filed in one place, so that a fragment still yields the picture. Hinton will spend fifty years building machines on exactly that principle, representations distributed across many units, no single one of which holds the thing. He tells the story often. Nobody wrote it down at the time.

Physics and chemistry, then physiology, then philosophy, then architecture, then back again, before he takes his degree in experimental psychology in 1970. What the psychologists teach him about the brain strikes him as thin, mostly rats and reflexes, with nothing in it that explains how a thought could also be a physical event. The Unit's tradition is applied and empirical: how a pilot misreads a dial under load, how a word is retrieved or lost, what a tired operator does wrong. From inside it, on a civil servant's salary, Hinton goes on writing about how a network might hold a concept without storing that concept anywhere in particular. He stays two years to the month.

It is one of the few departments in America where a machine that learns from examples is not treated as a curiosity to be indulged. He works with Terrence Sejnowski on a network built out of statistical mechanics rather than logic, and with David Rumelhart on the problem that has blocked the entire approach since Minsky and Papert: in a network with hidden layers, how does any unit find out what it should have done differently?

stops.campa: With David Ackley and Terrence Sejnowski he publishes a learning algorithm for what they name the Boltzmann machine: a network whose units switch on and off with a probability borrowed from statistical physics, settling toward low-energy configurations the way a cooling metal settles into an arrangement of its atoms. Shown examples from a domain, it learns the constraints that hold in that domain without being told what they are. The distribution the name comes from is Ludwig Boltzmann's. The paper appears in Cognitive Science in 1985.

stops.campa: With David Rumelhart and Ronald Williams he publishes in Nature a way of training networks with hidden layers: send the error backward through the layers and adjust each weight in proportion to what it contributed. The units in the middle, which nobody has told what to represent, discover useful features by themselves. The mathematics is not new and Hinton says so in public for the next forty years. Seppo Linnainmaa had the reverse-mode procedure in 1970, Paul Werbos applied it to networks in 1974. The 1986 contribution is the demonstration, in a journal everybody reads. The paper runs to four pages.

Hinton's networks are that principle carried into arithmetic, with a procedure for assigning credit which Hebb never had and did not claim to need.
